plan.title: How this course takes you from band 4 to 8+
paras: Five levels: Foundation (4.0 → 5.0), Developing (5.0 → 6.0), Competent (6.0 → 7.0), Advanced (7.0 → 7.5) and Expert (7.5 → 8.0+). Every unit trains all four skills around one common IELTS topic: academic vocabulary, Speaking Parts 1–3, a reading passage with True / False / Not Given, two grammar structures and a timed Writing task with a model answer.

Pace: one unit every 3–4 days, about 45–60 minutes a day, plus the outside practice listed under each level. From band 4.0, reaching 8.0 usually takes 18–24 months of steady work. Moving up one full band generally needs a few hundred hours of focused practice in total.

Honest note: no website can guarantee a band score. This course builds the vocabulary, grammar, speaking fluency and essay structure that high bands need. To reach 8.0–9.0 you must also do timed Cambridge IELTS practice tests, read long academic texts, listen to native-speed English every day, and get your Writing and Speaking marked by a qualified teacher.
Model answers and their band labels are written by desktopchill as study references. They are not official, examiner-marked scripts.
weeks: Everyday topics. Answer Part 1 questions with a reason and an example; describe simple tables; write a clear four-paragraph opinion essay.
Society topics. Extend Part 3 answers; describe trends accurately; plan discussion and problem–solution essays; reduce basic grammar errors.
Abstract topics. Use less common vocabulary and complex sentences with control; handle every Task 1 chart type; build cohesive arguments.
Precision. Collocations, hedging and nuance; Part 3 speculation and evaluation; essays with fully developed, well-supported ideas.
Exam conditions. A full mock test every week, teacher feedback on Writing and Speaking, and fixing the last error patterns.
When you score 8.0 or higher on three Cambridge practice tests in a row under real timing, and a teacher rates your Writing and Speaking at 7.5 or above.

gram.title: Present simple vs present continuous
gram.rule: Present simple: facts and habits (I live, it rains) · Present continuous: now / temporary / changing (I am living, it is growing)
gram.note: Use the present simple for permanent facts and routines: My city has two universities. Use the present continuous for actions happening now, temporary situations and trends: More people are moving to the suburbs. Verbs like know, like, want are rarely continuous.

cue.card: Describe a place in your hometown that you like.
points: and explain why you like it
model: I’d like to talk about West Lake Park, which is only ten minutes from my house. It’s a large park with a lake in the middle, lots of old trees and a path that goes all the way around the water.

In the early morning it’s full of local residents. Older people do tai chi, some people go jogging, and in the evening families come to walk and buy ice cream. At weekends there are often small music performances near the gate.

I like it for two reasons. First, it’s the most peaceful place in my neighbourhood. The streets around it are crowded and noisy, but once you are inside, you can hear birds. Second, it has a lot of memories for me, because my grandfather taught me to ride a bike there. Whenever I feel stressed, I go there for a walk and I always feel better afterwards.

write.prompt: The table below shows the population of three cities in 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
write.data:
City        2000 (millions)   2020 (millions)
City A      2.1               4.0
City B      3.5               3.9
City C      1.2               1.0
plan: Introduction: paraphrase the task (shows → illustrates; population → number of residents)
Overview: two main features — A grew fastest; C was the only city to shrink
Body 1: City A and City B with exact figures
Body 2: City C, and one comparison across all three
model: The table illustrates how many people lived in three cities, A, B and C, in 2000 and 2020.
Overall, the populations of City A and City B increased over the period, with City A showing by far the biggest rise. City C was the only city whose population fell.

In 2000, City A had 2.1 million residents, which was fewer than City B. However, over the next twenty years its population almost doubled to 4 million, making it the largest of the three cities by 2020. City B started with the highest figure, 3.5 million, and grew only slightly, reaching 3.9 million in 2020.

City C was the smallest city in both years. Its population went down from 1.2 million to 1 million, a drop of around 17 per cent. As a result, by 2020 City A was four times bigger than City C, whereas in 2000 the difference between them had been much smaller.

cue.card: Describe a job you would like to do in the future.
points: how you could get this job
and explain why you would like to do it
model: In the future, I’d really like to work as a project manager for large construction projects, such as bridges or hospitals.

This job needs a mix of technical and people skills. You need engineering knowledge to understand the drawings, but you also need to communicate clearly, plan schedules and solve problems quickly when something goes wrong on site.

To get this job, I think I need two or three more years of experience as an engineer first. I’m also planning to take a project management qualification, and of course my English has to be much better, because many big projects involve foreign partners.

The main reason I’d like to do it is that I enjoy seeing the whole picture. At the moment I only work on one part of a building. As a project manager, I could lead a team and see a project from the first drawing to the opening day, which I think would give me a lot of satisfaction.

write.prompt: Some people think that universities should focus on practical skills for work. Others believe that the main purpose of university is to give students knowledge. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
plan: Introduction: paraphrase both views and give your opinion (both matter, but knowledge comes first)
Body 1: why practical skills matter — employers, internships, example
Body 2: why knowledge matters — deep understanding, changing jobs, example
Conclusion: restate your opinion in one or two sentences
model: Some people argue that universities should mainly prepare students for the workplace, while others think their key role is to provide knowledge. In my view, both are important, but a strong foundation of knowledge should come first.

On the one hand, practical skills help graduates find jobs. Many employers complain that new graduates know a lot of theory but cannot use software, write a clear report or work in a team. If universities include internships and real projects, students can gain experience before they graduate. For example, engineering students who spend a semester at a construction company often get job offers from the same company.

On the other hand, the main value of a degree is deep knowledge that lasts for a long time. Practical skills change quickly; a computer program that students learn today may be out of date in five years. However, a student who really understands the principles of physics or economics can learn new tools easily. In addition, universities are places for research and critical thinking, not only for job training.

In conclusion, although practical skills are clearly useful, I believe universities should focus first on giving students solid knowledge, and then add practical training on top of it. This combination will prepare graduates not only for their first job but for a whole career.

write.prompt: The bar chart below shows how many hours per week people in four age groups spent on three leisure activities. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
write.data:
Hours per week   16–24   25–39   40–59   60+
Social media      14      9       5       2
Sport             5       3       2       2
Reading           2       3       4       7
plan: Introduction: paraphrase (bar chart, hours per week, age groups)
Overview: social media falls with age, reading rises with age
Body 1: social media and sport across the groups
Body 2: reading, and the over-60s compared with the youngest group
model: The bar chart compares the number of hours per week that people in four age groups spent on social media, sport and reading.
Overall, time spent on social media fell sharply as people got older, while reading showed the opposite pattern. Sport was the least time-consuming activity for every group except the oldest.

The 16–24 group spent 14 hours a week on social media, which was the highest figure in the chart. This dropped to 9 hours for people aged 25–39, 5 hours for those aged 40–59 and only 2 hours for the over-60s. Young people also did the most sport, at 5 hours a week, compared with 2 or 3 hours in the other groups.

In contrast, reading increased steadily with age. The youngest group read for just 2 hours a week, but this rose to 4 hours for people in their forties and fifties and reached 7 hours among the over-60s. In fact, people over 60 spent more than three times as long reading as they did on social media.

write.prompt: In many countries, young adults now live independently instead of with their parents. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase and state your view (advantages outweigh disadvantages)
Body 1: disadvantages — cost, loneliness, less support for parents
Body 2: advantages — independence, skills, relationships; stronger point
Conclusion: restate your view
model: In many parts of the world, it is becoming more common for young adults to move out of their parents’ home and live on their own. Although this trend has some drawbacks, I believe its benefits are greater.

There are certainly some disadvantages. Firstly, living alone is expensive. Young people have to pay rent and bills, so they may save less money than if they stayed at home. Secondly, some young adults feel lonely, especially if they move to a new city for work. Finally, when children leave home, their parents may receive less help, which can be a problem as they get older.

However, the advantages are more significant. The most important one is personal development. When young people live independently, they have to cook, manage a budget and solve problems by themselves, and these skills make them more confident adults. In addition, living apart can actually improve family relationships. Many people find that they get on better with their parents when they visit at weekends instead of arguing about small things every day. Moreover, with modern technology, it is easy to keep in touch and support each other from a distance.

In conclusion, while living independently costs more and can be lonely at first, I believe the advantages, especially the chance to become a mature and responsible adult, clearly outweigh the disadvantages.

cue.card: Describe a healthy habit you have.
points: and explain why you think it is healthy
model: One healthy habit I have is walking to work instead of taking a motorbike. I started it about a year ago, when my company moved to an office about two kilometres from my apartment.

At first I only did it because parking was expensive, but now I really enjoy it. It takes me about twenty-five minutes each way, so I walk almost an hour a day without having to find extra time for exercise.

It has affected my life in several positive ways. I sleep better, I have more energy in the morning, and I’ve lost about four kilos without changing my diet much. It also gives me time to think about my day or listen to English podcasts, which helps my listening skills.

I think it’s healthy because doctors recommend at least thirty minutes of physical activity every day, and most office workers sit for eight or nine hours. Walking is free, easy and safe, so I believe more people should try it, especially in cities with terrible traffic jams.

write.prompt: Fast food is becoming more and more popular. Why is this happening? What can be done to encourage people to eat healthier food?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase and outline the answer (causes + solutions)
Body 1: causes — busy lifestyles, price, advertising
Body 2: solutions — education in schools, labels and taxes, cheaper healthy options
Conclusion: summarise
model: In many countries, fast food is now part of everyday life. This essay will explain the main reasons for this trend and suggest some ways to encourage healthier eating.

There are several reasons why fast food is so popular. The first is the busy modern lifestyle. Many people work long hours and spend a lot of time commuting, so they do not have the time or energy to cook. Fast food is quick and available almost everywhere. Secondly, it is often cheap, which makes it attractive to students and young workers. Finally, fast-food companies spend huge amounts of money on advertising, especially on social media, and children are strongly influenced by these adverts.

However, there are a number of things that could be done. To begin with, schools should teach children how to cook simple, nutritious meals and explain the health risks of junk food. In addition, governments could make clear labels compulsory, so that people can see how much sugar, salt and fat a product contains. A tax on sugary drinks, like the ones introduced in several countries, could also reduce consumption. At the same time, cities could support small restaurants that sell healthy food at a fair price.
In conclusion, fast food is popular mainly because it is fast, cheap and heavily advertised. Better education, clearer information and financial measures could help people make healthier choices.

write.prompt: The table below shows the average monthly spending of a household in one city in 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
plan: Introduction: paraphrase (average monthly household spending, two years)
Overview: housing was the biggest cost and rose most; entertainment grew fastest in relative terms; transport was stable
Body 1: housing and food
Body 2: transport and entertainment, with a comparison
model: The table compares how much an average household in one city spent per month on four categories in 2010 and 2020.
Overall, housing was the largest expense in both years and saw the biggest increase in dollar terms. Spending on entertainment more than tripled, while transport costs changed very little.

In 2010, a household spent $300 a month on housing, but by 2020 this had risen to $520, an increase of more than 70 per cent. Food was the second largest category. It went up only slightly, from $250 to $280, so by 2020 households were spending almost twice as much on housing as on food.

Transport was the only category that fell, dropping from $120 to $110 a month. In contrast, spending on entertainment grew dramatically, from just $40 to $130. As a result, in 2020 households spent more on entertainment than on transport, whereas ten years earlier the opposite had been true.

cue.card: Describe a memorable trip you took.
points: and explain why it was memorable
model: I’d like to describe a trip to Ha Giang, in the far north of Vietnam, which I took with three university friends two years ago.

We rented motorbikes in Ha Giang city and spent four days riding along the mountain roads. Our itinerary was quite simple: we rode in the morning, stopped at small villages for lunch, and stayed in family homestays at night, so the accommodation was very cheap.

The scenery was absolutely breathtaking, especially the Ma Pi Leng Pass, where the road runs along the edge of a deep valley. We also visited a local market where people from different ethnic groups came to buy and sell animals and food.

It was memorable for two reasons. First, it was the first long trip I planned completely by myself, without a package holiday. Second, something went wrong: on the third day it was raining heavily and one of the bikes broke down. A family let us stay in their house and cooked dinner for us. That kindness is the thing I remember most.

write.prompt: Tourism brings many benefits to a country, but it also causes problems. Do you think the advantages of tourism outweigh the disadvantages?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase and give your opinion (advantages outweigh, if managed)
Body 1: disadvantages — overcrowding, pollution, rising prices
Body 2: advantages — jobs and income, culture and infrastructure
Conclusion: restate and add the condition (good management)
model: Tourism has become one of the world’s largest industries. Although it can create serious problems, I believe its advantages are greater, as long as it is managed carefully.

There is no doubt that tourism can have negative effects. Famous destinations often become overcrowded, especially in the peak season, which damages the experience for both visitors and residents. Large numbers of tourists also produce rubbish and pollution, and beaches and forests can be harmed. Moreover, when many visitors arrive, the prices of food and housing tend to rise, so local people may struggle to afford them.

Nevertheless, the benefits of tourism are more significant. Above all, it creates jobs, not only in hotels and restaurants but also for farmers, drivers and craftspeople. In poor rural areas, money from tourism can be the main source of income for whole villages. In addition, tourism encourages governments to build better roads, airports and other facilities that local people also use. Finally, it promotes cultural exchange, as visitors learn about local traditions and residents meet people from around the world.

In conclusion, while tourism can lead to overcrowding, pollution and higher prices, I believe these problems can be reduced through good planning, such as limiting visitor numbers at sensitive sites. Therefore, the economic and cultural advantages of tourism outweigh its disadvantages.

cue.card: Describe a piece of technology you find useful.
points: and explain why it is useful to you
model: The piece of technology I find most useful is actually quite simple: a pair of wireless headphones with noise cancelling. I got them as a birthday present from my sister about a year ago.

I use them every single day. In the morning I listen to podcasts while I’m commuting on the bus, and at work I use them for video calls with clients. In the evening I sometimes wear them just to have some silence while I read, because my street is very noisy.

They are useful to me for three reasons. First, they help me concentrate. Our office is open-plan, and before I had them the noise was a real distraction. Second, they have improved my English, since I now listen to about an hour of English podcasts a day. And third, they make my commute much more relaxing.
The only drawback is that I sometimes forget to charge them. But overall, I think they were the best present I’ve ever received, and I can’t imagine my daily routine without them now.

write.prompt: Some people think that the internet has brought people closer together. Others think it has made people more isolated. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
plan: Introduction: paraphrase both views; opinion — closer, if used carefully
Body 1: isolation — screen time replaces real contact, comparison and loneliness
Body 2: closer — distance, communities, families abroad
Conclusion: balanced but clear opinion
model: The internet has changed the way people communicate. While some believe it has brought people closer, others argue that it has made them more isolated. In my opinion, it mostly connects people, but only if it is used sensibly.

On the one hand, there are good reasons to think that the internet makes people lonely. Many people spend hours scrolling through social media instead of meeting friends face to face. Even when families eat together, everyone may be looking at a screen. Furthermore, social media often shows perfect versions of other people’s lives, which can make users feel that they are missing out. Some studies have linked heavy social media use with loneliness, especially among teenagers.

On the other hand, the internet allows people to stay in touch in ways that were impossible before. Millions of Vietnamese workers and students live abroad, and video calls let them see their families every day for free. The internet also helps people with the same interests find each other, for example in online groups for new parents or for people with rare illnesses. For many people, these online communities lead to real friendships.

In conclusion, I believe the internet has brought people closer together overall, because it removes distance as a barrier to communication. However, it should support face-to-face relationships rather than replace them.

points: what you see or do on the way
and explain how you feel about this journey

write.prompt: The bar chart below shows the main ways people travelled to work in one city in 2005 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
write.data:
% of commuters     2005    2025
Motorbike          65      48
Car                 5      14
Bus/Metro          10      24
Walking/Cycling    20      14
plan: Introduction: paraphrase (percentage of commuters, four modes, two years)
Overview: motorbikes most popular both years but fell; public transport and cars rose
Body 1: motorbikes and walking/cycling (falls)
Body 2: bus/metro and car (rises), with a comparison
model: The bar chart shows the percentage of commuters in one city who used four different types of transport to get to work in 2005 and 2025.

Overall, the motorbike was the most common way to travel to work in both years, although its share fell considerably. By contrast, public transport and cars became much more popular over the twenty-year period.

In 2005, almost two thirds of commuters (65%) travelled by motorbike, but this figure had dropped to less than half (48%) by 2025. Walking and cycling also became less popular, falling from 20% to 14% of journeys.

At the same time, the proportion of people using buses or the metro more than doubled, from 10% to 24%, which made public transport the second most popular option in 2025. The share of commuters who drove a car also rose sharply, from just 5% to 14%. As a result, in 2025 cars were used as often as walking and cycling combined had been used in the past for short commutes, which suggests that the city’s roads became busier with larger vehicles.

I didn’t have a ticket to the stadium, so I watched it with about twenty colleagues on a big screen at a café near our office. The atmosphere was incredible. Everyone was wearing red shirts, and the spectators in the café were shouting and singing as if they were in the stadium.

The match was very tense. Thailand scored first, and for a long time it looked like we would lose. Then, about ten minutes before the end, Vietnam scored twice in five minutes. When the final whistle blew, people ran out into the street, waving flags and riding their motorbikes around the city.

I felt really proud and happy, and also a bit surprised at how emotional I was, because I don’t normally care that much about football. I think the reason it was so memorable is that sport brings people together. For one evening, everyone in that café felt like one big team.

write.prompt: Some people believe that children should spend more time doing sports at school, while others think academic subjects are more important. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
plan: Introduction: paraphrase both views; opinion — more sport, without cutting core subjects
Body 1: academic subjects — exams, careers, limited time
Body 2: sport — health, concentration, teamwork
Conclusion: restate opinion
model: There is an ongoing debate about whether schools should give more time to sport or concentrate on academic subjects. Although academic study is clearly essential, I believe children should do more sport at school.

Those who prefer academic subjects argue that school time is limited and that maths, languages and science are the key to future success. Students must pass important exams, and their results often decide which university or job they can get. From this point of view, extra hours of sport might mean less time for the subjects that really count.

However, there are strong arguments for more physical education. Firstly, many children today have a sedentary lifestyle, spending hours in front of screens, and childhood obesity is rising in many countries. Regular sport at school is the only exercise some children get. Secondly, research suggests that physical activity improves concentration and memory, so it may actually help academic performance. Finally, team sports teach skills that classrooms cannot easily teach, such as teamwork, leadership and how to deal with failure.

In conclusion, while academic subjects must remain the main focus of education, I believe schools should provide at least one hour of physical activity every day. Healthy, active children are likely to learn better and become more well-rounded adults.

cue.card: Describe a time when the weather changed your plans.
points: and explain how you felt about it
model: I’d like to talk about a weekend last October, when a storm completely changed my plans.
My friends and I had planned a camping trip to a lake about two hours from Hanoi. We had booked a campsite, bought food and borrowed tents. The forecast earlier in the week said it would be sunny.

However, on Friday evening the forecast suddenly changed. A tropical storm was moving towards the coast, and heavy rain was expected across the north. By Saturday morning it was pouring, and the wind was so strong that some trees in my street fell down. Parts of the road to the lake were flooded, so we had no choice but to cancel.

At first I felt really disappointed, because we had been looking forward to it for weeks. But in the end we had a great time anyway. We moved the “camping trip” to my apartment, cooked the barbecue food in the kitchen and watched films all evening. Looking back, I’m glad we stayed home, because the storm caused a lot of damage that weekend.

write.prompt: The table below shows the amount of household waste recycled in four countries in 2012 and 2022 (as a percentage of all household waste). Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
write.data:
Country     2012    2022
Country A   45%     62%
Country B   30%     35%
Country C   12%     28%
Country D   20%     18%
plan: Introduction: paraphrase (proportion of household waste recycled, four countries, two years)
Overview: three countries improved; A highest; D the only fall
Body 1: A and B
Body 2: C and D, with comparisons
model: The table shows what proportion of household waste was recycled in four countries in 2012 and 2022.
Overall, recycling rates rose in three of the four countries, and Country A recycled the largest share of its waste in both years. Country D was the only country where the rate fell.

In 2012, Country A already recycled 45% of its household waste, and this figure increased to 62% ten years later, meaning that almost two thirds of its waste was recycled. Country B started at 30%, but it improved only slightly, reaching 35% in 2022.

The most dramatic change was in Country C, where the recycling rate more than doubled, from just 12% to 28%. As a result, it moved from last place to third. Country D, by contrast, recycled 20% of its waste in 2012, but this dropped slightly to 18% in 2022, so by the end of the period it had the lowest rate of the four countries.

cue.card: Describe a film you enjoyed watching.
points: when and where you watched it
and explain why you enjoyed it
model: I’d like to talk about a documentary called “My Octopus Teacher”, which I watched on a streaming service about two years ago.

I watched it at home on a rainy Sunday afternoon with my younger sister. Neither of us expected much, because it was recommended by an algorithm, not by a friend, but it turned out to be one of the most memorable films I’ve seen.

It’s about a man in South Africa who was going through a difficult time in his life. He started diving every day in a kelp forest near his home, and he slowly built a relationship with a wild octopus. The film follows the octopus for about a year, showing how it hunts, hides from sharks and finally grows old.

I enjoyed it for two reasons. First, the photography was breathtaking. I had never realised how intelligent octopuses are. Second, the story was inspiring. It showed how spending time in nature helped the man recover from stress. After watching it, I started going for walks in the park more often, so I guess it had a real effect on me.

write.prompt: Many people now get their news from social media rather than from newspapers or television. Is this a positive or negative development?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase; position — mainly negative
Body 1: positives — speed, free, different voices (concede)
Body 2: negatives — fake news, headlines only, filter bubbles (main argument)
Conclusion: restate and suggest media literacy
model: Nowadays, a growing number of people read the news on social media instead of in newspapers or on television. Although this development has some benefits, I believe it is mainly negative.

It is true that social media has made news faster and more accessible. Important stories can reach millions of people within minutes, and most of this information is free. In addition, social media allows ordinary people to share what is happening around them, so we can hear voices that traditional media may ignore. For example, during floods, local residents often post useful updates before journalists arrive.

However, the disadvantages are more serious. The biggest problem is fake news. On social media, anyone can publish a story, and false information often spreads faster than the truth because it is more shocking. Secondly, many users only read headlines or watch short videos, so they get a very simple picture of complicated issues. Finally, social media platforms show people content that matches what they already like, which means users rarely see different opinions. Over time, this can make society more divided.

In conclusion, although getting news from social media is fast and convenient, I believe it is a negative trend overall because it encourages misinformation and shallow understanding. Schools should therefore teach young people how to check sources and think critically about what they read online.
